transcript.en: You record study minutes in seven variables, Monday to Sunday. Adding them up takes one long line. Then your tutor asks for the whole month: thirty names. Can one name hold them all? By the end, you’ll be able to keep many numbers under one name, reach any one, and add them up. On paper, you’d write the week in one row, under one heading: Week. To find Thursday, you count along from Monday. One heading, seven values, in order. Python calls this a list: values in order, under one name, between square brackets. Week gets a list of seven numbers. One name now holds the whole week, and it could hold a month. Each value has a place, its index, counted from zero. So week at zero is Monday’s thirty, and week at three is Thursday’s sixty. Week at minus one counts back from the end: Sunday’s ninety. To add up the week, a for loop visits every value in order. Each turn, m holds the next value, and total grows, to two hundred and fifty. The built-in sum gives the same total. Lists can grow. Week dot append, forty, adds a value at the end. Now the length of week is eight, so a month can grow one day at a time. Quick check! A list holds three marks: seventy, eighty-five and ninety. What does marks at index one give? Eighty-five. Indexes count from zero, so index one is the second value. Index three would stop the program with an IndexError: three values have indexes zero, one and two. Lists fit anything kept in order: a week of readings, the names in a queue, the rooms you booked this term. Not a list: seven separate variables. No loop can visit them one by one. In the app, open Step through a program and press Change the code. Type the week’s list, total and the loop. Press Run and record, and before each Next, say what m and total hold. Watch for two hundred and fifty. Your turn. Seven variables for a week, thirty for a month. Can one name hold them all? Yes: one list holds the whole month, in order. Remember: a list keeps many values in order under one name. An index counts from zero, so the first value is at zero. And a for loop visits every value, while append adds one at the end. Try it yourself: put this week’s study minutes in a list, then print the total and your best day’s minutes. Next lesson: finding a value by its name, not its place.

body.en:
You record study minutes in seven variables, Monday to Sunday, and adding them up takes one long line. A month would need thirty names. A list solves it: one name holds many values, in order, and a loop can visit every one of them.

A list is written between square brackets, with commas between its values: week = [30, 45, 0, 60, 25, 0, 90]. Each value has an index, its place, counted from zero: week[0] is Monday's 30 and week[3] is Thursday's 60. Negative indexes count back from the end, so week[-1] is Sunday's 90. len(week) is 7, so the last index is len(week) - 1, which is 6, and week[7] stops the program with IndexError: list index out of range. week[1] = 50 replaces one value.

for m in week: gives m each value in turn. With total = 0 before the loop and total = total + m inside it, the week adds up to 250. sum(week) gives the same 250, max(week) 90 and min(week) 0. week.append(40) adds a value at the end, so len(week) becomes 8. 60 in week is True: in looks through the values one by one. And split cuts a string into a list at each comma: "LAB-001,scale,B12".split(",") gives ["LAB-001", "scale", "B12"].

Watch for two traps. The first value is at index 0, not 1. And backup = items does not copy a list: it gives the same list a second name, so backup.append("scale") changes items too. For a separate list, write backup = items.copy().
body.ar:
تسجّل دقائق مذاكرتك في سبعة متغيّرات، من الاثنين إلى الأحد، وجمعها يحتاج إلى سطر واحد طويل. والشهر سيحتاج إلى ثلاثين اسمًا. والحل هو القائمة (list): اسم واحد يحمل قيمًا كثيرة بالترتيب، وتستطيع حلقة أن تمرّ عليها كلها.

تُكتب القائمة بين قوسين مربعين، وبين قيمها فواصل: ⁦week = [30, 45, 0, 60, 25, 0, 90]⁩. ولكل قيمة فهرس (index)، أي موضعها، يُعدّ من صفر: ⁦week[0]⁩ هي 30 يوم الاثنين، و⁦week[3]⁩ هي 60 يوم الخميس. والفهارس السالبة تعدّ من النهاية، فـ ⁦week[-1]⁩ هي 90 يوم الأحد. و⁦len(week)⁩ تساوي 7، فآخر فهرس هو ⁦len(week) - 1⁩ أي 6، و⁦week[7]⁩ توقف البرنامج برسالة IndexError: list index out of range. أما ⁦week[1] = 50⁩ فتستبدل قيمة واحدة.

تعطي for m in week: المتغيّر m كل قيمة بدورها. ومع ⁦total = 0⁩ قبل الحلقة و⁦total = total + m⁩ داخلها، يصل مجموع الأسبوع إلى 250. وتعطي ⁦sum(week)⁩ المجموع نفسه 250، و⁦max(week)⁩ القيمة 90، و⁦min(week)⁩ القيمة 0. وتضيف ⁦week.append(40)⁩ قيمة في النهاية، فتصبح ⁦len(week)⁩ مساوية 8. و60 in week تساوي True: فـ in تفحص القيم واحدة واحدة. أما split فتقطع النص إلى قائمة عند كل فاصلة: ⁦"LAB-001,scale,B12".split(",")⁩ تعطي ⁦["LAB-001", "scale", "B12"]⁩.

انتبه لفخّين. أول قيمة عند الفهرس 0 لا 1. و⁦backup = items⁩ لا تنسخ القائمة، بل تعطي القائمة نفسها اسمًا ثانيًا، فتغيّر ⁦backup.append("scale")⁩ القائمة items أيضًا. ولتحصل على قائمة منفصلة اكتب ⁦backup = items.copy()⁩.

transcript.en: The lab keeps its stock in two lists. Item names are in one, counts in the other. To find the projectors, you search one and count along the other. Why can’t you just ask for projectors? By the end, you’ll be able to find a value by its name, not its place, and count how often things appear. A stock book works the other way. Open it at Projectors, and the count sits beside the name. The name takes you straight to the number. Python calls this a dictionary: pairs of a key and a value, between curly brackets. The key is what you ask for, projector, and the value is what you find, three. Stock of projector gives three. Lend two, and stock of projector gets two: the new value replaces the old one. Give it a new key, scale, and a pair is added. Ask for a missing key, kettle, and the program stops with a KeyError. Get asks safely: get with kettle and zero gives zero. So counting is one line: each room’s count gets its count so far, or zero, plus one. Items gives each key with its value, as a pair in round brackets: a tuple. Loop over the sorted pairs, and the rooms come out in order. Sort when order matters: a computer keeps the order keys arrived, your phone doesn’t. Quick check! Marks holds Omar with seventy-two and Sara with sixty-four. Then Omar gets eighty. What do the length of marks and Omar’s mark show? Two and eighty. A key appears only once, so Omar’s new value replaces seventy-two. Marks still holds two pairs. Dictionaries fit any lookup by name: prices by item, a timetable by day, marks by student number. Not a dictionary: a week of readings, where order and repeats matter. That stays a list. In the app, open Step through a program and press Change the code. Type the rooms, an empty counts and the counting loop. Press Run and record; before each Next, say what counts holds. Watch B12 reach three. Your turn. The lab’s stock sits in two lists, names in one and counts in the other. Why can’t you just ask for projectors? Because a list finds values by place, not by name. Remember: a dictionary keeps pairs of a key and a value. Ask for a key that may be missing with get. And sort the pairs to report in order. Try it yourself: count the letters of your name with a dictionary, and print them in sorted order. Next lesson: choosing a list, a dictionary or a set, and counting the work.

title.en: Find a value by its name

body.en:
The lab's stock sits in two lists, item names in one and counts in the other. To find the projectors you search the names, then count along the counts, because a list finds values by their place. A dictionary finds them by a name.

A dictionary holds pairs of a key and a value, between curly brackets: stock = {"laptop": 12, "projector": 3}. stock["projector"] looks up the value of the key "projector": 3. stock["projector"] = 2 replaces that value, and stock["scale"] = 5 adds a new pair. A key appears only once, so giving it a value again replaces the old one; len(stock) counts the pairs, now 3. A value can be anything: a number, a string, even a list.

Asking for a missing key, stock["kettle"], stops the program with a KeyError (on your phone the last line reads KeyError: kettle; a computer writes KeyError: 'kettle'). Ask safely: "kettle" in stock checks the keys, not the values, and gives False, while stock.get("kettle", 0) gives the value, or 0 when the key is missing. Counting is then one line: counts[r] = counts.get(r, 0) + 1 adds one to r's count, starting from 0 the first time r appears.

stock.items() gives each key with its value as a pair, ("laptop", 12): a pair in round brackets is a tuple, and for item, n in stock.items(): puts its two parts into two names. enumerate(week, start=1) gives pairs too: (1, 30), (2, 45). keys() and values() give the keys or the values alone. A computer's Python keeps a dictionary in the order its keys were added; your phone's doesn't, and even a printed dictionary can come out in another order. So sort when order matters: for room, n in sorted(counts.items()): gives the rooms in order.
body.ar:
مخزون المعمل في قائمتين، أسماء الأصناف في واحدة والأعداد في الأخرى. ولكي تجد البروجكتورات تبحث في الأسماء، ثم تعدّ في قائمة الأعداد، لأن القائمة تجد القيم بموضعها. أما القاموس فيجدها باسم.

يحمل القاموس (dictionary) أزواجًا، كل زوج مفتاح (key) وقيمة، بين أقواس معقوفة: ⁦stock = {"laptop": 12, "projector": 3}⁩. وتبحث ⁦stock["projector"]⁩ عن قيمة المفتاح ⁦"projector": 3⁩. وتستبدل ⁦stock["projector"] = 2⁩ تلك القيمة، وتضيف ⁦stock["scale"] = 5⁩ زوجًا جديدًا. ويظهر المفتاح مرة واحدة فقط، فإعطاؤه قيمة من جديد يستبدل القديمة، وتعدّ ⁦len(stock)⁩ الأزواج، وهي الآن 3. ويمكن أن تكون القيمة أي شيء: عددًا أو نصًّا، بل قائمة.

طلب مفتاح غير موجود، ⁦stock["kettle"]⁩، يوقف البرنامج برسالة KeyError (ويقول السطر الأخير على هاتفك KeyError: kettle، ويكتب الحاسوب ⁦KeyError: 'kettle'⁩). فاسأل بأمان: ⁦"kettle" in stock⁩ تفحص المفاتيح لا القيم، وتعطي False، بينما تعطي ⁦stock.get("kettle", 0)⁩ القيمة، أو 0 إن لم يكن المفتاح موجودًا. وهكذا يصير العدّ سطرًا واحدًا: ⁦counts[r] = counts.get(r, 0) + 1⁩ تضيف واحدًا إلى عدد r، بدءًا من 0 في أول مرة يظهر فيها r.

تعطي ⁦stock.items()⁩ كل مفتاح مع قيمته زوجًا، ⁦("laptop", 12)⁩: والزوج بين قوسين عاديين اسمه tuple، وتضع ⁦for item, n in stock.items()⁩: جزأيه في اسمين. وتعطي ⁦enumerate(week, start=1)⁩ أزواجًا أيضًا: ⁦(1, 30)⁩ و⁦(2, 45)⁩. وتعطي ⁦keys()⁩ و⁦values()⁩ المفاتيح وحدها أو القيم وحدها. وتحفظ Python على الحاسوب القاموس بترتيب إضافة مفاتيحه، أما على هاتفك فلا، وقد يظهر القاموس المطبوع بترتيب آخر. فرتّب حين يهمّ الترتيب: ⁦for room, n in sorted(counts.items())⁩: تعطي القاعات مرتّبة.

transcript.en: Two programs check the lab’s equipment tags for duplicates. With eleven tags, both answer at once. With two thousand, one takes a thousand times the work of the other. Both are correct, so what is the slow one doing? By the end, you’ll be able to choose where to keep your data, and count the work two methods cost. Picture eleven name cards: is any name there twice? You could hold each card against every other card. Or keep a sheet of names seen, and glance at it once per card. Each comparison or glance is one step. The number of steps a method takes is its step count. We count steps, not seconds, because seconds change from phone to phone. The first way is a loop inside a loop. For each tag, the inner loop compares it with every tag after it. Eleven tags make ten, then nine, and so on: fifty-five comparisons. The second way keeps a set: a collection with no repeats that answers one question fast. Have I seen this tag? Checking a set is a lookup: it goes straight to where the tag would be. One lookup per tag: eleven steps. Now grow the list. A thousand and one tags make five hundred thousand, five hundred pairs. Two thousand make one million, nine hundred and ninety-nine thousand. One lookup each is just two thousand. Quick check! Now the seen tags go in a list instead of a set. With two thousand tags, about how much work is that? Up to about two million. In on a list checks the items one by one: a hidden second loop. A set or a dictionary goes straight to the tag. Choose by the job. Readings in order, with repeats: a list. Marks found by student number: a dictionary. Have I seen this tag: a set. A printed register needs order, so not a set. In the app, open Why an index is fast, where a school office finds pupils. Press Run under Watch one lookup and count the looks. Then choose one million rows and press Look up twenty pupils: half a million looks, or about twenty. Your turn. Eleven tags: both instant. Two thousand tags: one does a thousand times the work. What is the slow one doing? Comparing every tag with every other: nearly two million steps, against two thousand lookups. Remember: count steps, not seconds. When tags double, every pair grows four times, while one lookup each only doubles. And a set looks up in about one step. Try it yourself: add a counter to both duplicate checks, and run them on ten tags, then a hundred. Next lesson: an equipment inventory that refuses duplicates.

title.en: Count the steps before you choose

body.en:
Two programs check the lab's equipment tags for duplicates. Both are right, and with eleven tags both answer at once, but with two thousand one does about a thousand times the work. Seconds change from phone to phone, so we compare methods by their step count: how many basic steps, comparisons or lookups, each one takes.

The first way compares every pair with a nested loop, a loop inside a loop: for i in range(len(tags)): and inside it for j in range(i + 1, len(tags)):, so each tag meets every tag after it once. For n tags that is n × (n − 1) / 2 comparisons: 55 for 11 tags, 500,500 for 1,001 and 1,999,000 for 2,000. When the tags double, this count grows about four times.

The second way keeps a set of the tags seen so far. A set holds values with no repeats: seen = set() makes an empty one, seen.add(tag) adds a value, set(tags) makes one from a list, and tag in seen asks “have I seen this?” in about one step. That is a lookup: it goes straight to where the tag would be. One lookup per tag is 11, 1,001 or 2,000 steps, so doubling the tags only doubles it. len(seen) counts the different tags. A set keeps no order, and your phone prints it in any order, so print sorted(seen). A dictionary looks up its keys the same way.

Watch for a hidden loop: tag in a list is not one step, because in checks a list's items one by one. Keep the seen tags in a list, and the second way is as slow as the first. Choose by the job: a list for order and repeats, a dictionary to find or count by a key, a set for “have I seen this?”. For twenty values, write the clearest code: step counts matter as the data grows.
body.ar:
يفحص برنامجان رموز أجهزة المعمل بحثًا عن التكرار. كلاهما صحيح، ومع أحد عشر رمزًا يجيبان فورًا، لكن مع ألفين يعمل أحدهما نحو ألف ضعف ما يعمله الآخر. والثواني تختلف من هاتف إلى آخر، لذلك نقارن الطرق بعدد الخطوات (step count): كم خطوة أساسية، مقارنةً أو بحثًا، تأخذ كلٌّ منها.

تقارن الطريقة الأولى كل زوجين بحلقة متداخلة، أي حلقة داخل حلقة: ⁦for i in range(len(tags))⁩: وفي داخلها ⁦for j in range(i + 1, len(tags))⁩:، فيلتقي كل رمز بكل رمز بعده مرة واحدة. ولـ n رمز يكون ذلك ⁦n × (n − 1) / 2⁩ مقارنة: 55 لأحد عشر رمزًا، و500,500 لـ 1,001، و1,999,000 لـ 2,000. وحين يتضاعف عدد الرموز ينمو هذا العدد نحو أربع مرات.

أما الطريقة الثانية فتحفظ مجموعة (set) بالرموز التي رأيتها حتى الآن. والمجموعة تحمل قيمًا لا تكرار فيها: ⁦seen = set()⁩ تصنع مجموعة فارغة، و⁦seen.add(tag)⁩ تضيف قيمة، و⁦set(tags)⁩ تصنع مجموعة من قائمة، وtag in seen تسأل «هل رأيت هذا من قبل؟» في نحو خطوة واحدة. وهذا بحث مباشر (lookup): يذهب مباشرة إلى حيث يُفترض أن يكون الرمز. وبحث واحد لكل رمز يعني 11 أو 1,001 أو 2,000 خطوة، فمضاعفة الرموز تضاعفه فقط. وتعدّ ⁦len(seen)⁩ الرموز المختلفة. والمجموعة لا تحفظ ترتيبًا، ويطبعها هاتفك بأي ترتيب، فاطبع ⁦sorted(seen)⁩. والقاموس يبحث عن مفاتيحه بالطريقة نفسها.

انتبه للحلقة المخفية: tag in قائمة ليست خطوة واحدة، لأن in تفحص عناصر القائمة واحدًا واحدًا. فإن حفظت الرموز التي رأيتها في قائمة صارت الطريقة الثانية بطيئة مثل الأولى. واختر حسب المهمة: القائمة للترتيب والتكرار، والقاموس للبحث أو العدّ بمفتاح، والمجموعة لسؤال «هل رأيت هذا؟». ومع عشرين قيمة اكتب الكود الأوضح: فعدد الخطوات يهمّ كلما كبرت البيانات.

steps.solution:
n = int(input("How many tags? "))
seen = set()
for i in range(n):
    tag = input("Tag: ")
    if tag in seen:
        print("Repeat:", tag)
    seen.add(tag)
print("Different:", len(seen))

transcript.en: Someone enters a microscope: lab zero zero three, room B twelve. Next week, someone types lab zero zero three, small letters, room b twelve. Is that a second microscope, or the same one twice? And how would your program know? By the end, you’ll be able to build an inventory that tidies each entry, refuses repeats, and counts what each room holds. A careful clerk reads both lines as one microscope: capitals and stray spaces don’t change a tag. So she tidies every tag first, then compares. Bringing every value to one agreed form is called normalising. Strip the spaces, then upper for tags and rooms, lower for items. Normalise first, then compare. Each line splits at its commas into three parts. Normalised, they become a record: a dictionary with a tag, an item and a room. A line without exactly three parts gives None: it’s rejected, not guessed. The inventory is a dictionary keyed by tag. Before adding a record, look its tag up. If it’s already there, the new record is a duplicate: refuse it, note its line, and keep the first. To count by room, collect every record’s room in one line. That line is a list comprehension: room of r, for each r in the records. Then count the rooms with get. Quick check! Three sign-ups read S one two three, small s one two three, and S one two three with a space. After strip and upper, how many students? One. Strip and upper turn all three into capital S one two three. Normalise first, then compare, or one student counts three times. Anything people type needs this: email addresses in small letters, phone numbers without spaces, names stripped. Not a duplicate: two microscopes with different tags in one room. The item may repeat; the tag may not. In the app, open Cleaning a register, a school’s attendance sheet. Choose Tidy spaces and capitals, then Match the class list, and watch the names counted fall to eight. Now remove repeats: with names as typed, one is found; matched, three are. Your turn. Lab zero zero three in B twelve, then the same in small letters. A second microscope, or the same one twice? The same one: normalised, both tags match. Remember: turn each line into a record, and normalise before you compare. Key the inventory by tag, so a duplicate is one lookup away. And count with get, then report sorted. Try it yourself: list ten things in your room as tag, item and place, with two typed twice, differently. Then run your inventory. Next: the unit check.

body.en:
Someone enters a microscope as LAB-003, in room B12. A week later someone types lab-003, in small letters, room b12. It is the same microscope typed twice, but a program that compares the text as typed sees two. The fix is to normalise first: bring every value to one agreed form, then compare.

Each entry is typed TAG,ITEM,ROOM. line.split(",") cuts it into parts, strip() removes the spaces around each, upper() puts tags and rooms in capitals, and lower() puts items in small letters. The result is a record: a dictionary that describes one thing, {"tag": "LAB-003", "item": "microscope", "room": "B12"}. A line without exactly three parts, or with an empty part, is not guessed at: parse(line) returns None, and if rec is None: lets the program reject it and note its line number.

The inventory is a dictionary keyed by tag, so finding a tag is one lookup. Before adding a record, check if rec["tag"] in inventory:. If it is there, the new record is a duplicate: a record whose key, once normalised, is already taken. Keep the first, refuse the second and note its line. A second microscope with its own tag, LAB-007, is not a duplicate: items may repeat, tags may not. For 2,000 entries this check takes about 2,000 lookups.

A list comprehension builds a list in one line: [r["room"] for r in inventory.values()] gives every record's room, and [p.strip() for p in parts] strips every part at once. Add a condition to keep only some: [t for t in tags if t != ""]. Count the rooms with counts.get(room, 0) + 1, and report them with for room in sorted(counts):, because your phone doesn't keep a dictionary's order.
body.ar:
يسجّل أحدهم مجهرًا برمز LAB-003 في القاعة B12. وبعد أسبوع يكتب شخص آخر lab-003 بحروف صغيرة، والقاعة b12. إنه المجهر نفسه كُتب مرتين، لكن البرنامج الذي يقارن النص كما كُتب يرى مجهرين. والحل أن توحّد أولًا (normalise): أن تجعل كل قيمة بصيغة واحدة متفق عليها، ثم تقارن.

يُكتب كل إدخال بالشكل TAG,ITEM,ROOM. فتقطعه ⁦line.split(",")⁩ إلى أجزاء، وتحذف ⁦strip()⁩ المسافات حول كل جزء، وتجعل ⁦upper()⁩ الرموز والقاعات بحروف كبيرة، وتجعل ⁦lower()⁩ الأصناف بحروف صغيرة. والنتيجة سجلّ (record): قاموس يصف شيئًا واحدًا، ⁦{"tag": "LAB-003", "item": "microscope", "room": "B12"}⁩. أما السطر الذي ليس فيه ثلاثة أجزاء بالضبط، أو فيه جزء فارغ، فلا نخمّن معناه: تعيد ⁦parse(line)⁩ القيمة None، وتسمح if rec is None: للبرنامج بأن يرفضه ويسجّل رقم سطره.

الجرد قاموس مفاتيحه الرموز، فإيجاد رمز بحث مباشر واحد. وقبل إضافة سجلّ، افحص ⁦if rec["tag"] in inventory⁩:. فإن كان موجودًا فالسجلّ الجديد مكرّر (duplicate): سجلّ مفتاحه، بعد التوحيد، مأخوذ من قبل. احتفظ بالأول، وارفض الثاني وسجّل رقم سطره. أما مجهر ثانٍ له رمزه الخاص، LAB-007، فليس مكرّرًا: الأصناف قد تتكرّر، والرموز لا. ومع 2,000 إدخال يأخذ هذا الفحص نحو 2,000 بحث مباشر.

يبني list comprehension قائمة في سطر واحد: ⁦[r["room"] for r in inventory.values()]⁩ تعطي قاعة كل سجلّ، و⁦[p.strip() for p in parts]⁩ تحذف المسافات من كل الأجزاء مرة واحدة. وأضف شرطًا لتبقي بعضها فقط: [t for t in tags if t != ""]. ثم عُدّ القاعات بـ ⁦counts.get(room, 0) + 1⁩، واعرضها بـ ⁦for room in sorted(counts)⁩:، لأن هاتفك لا يحفظ ترتيب القاموس.

task.en: Build the equipment inventory with made-up data only. Entries are typed TAG,ITEM,ROOM, such as LAB-001,microscope,B12. Write four functions, each with a docstring: parse_entry(line) returns a record with tag and room in capitals and item in small letters, or None unless there are exactly three non-empty parts; add_record(inventory, record) adds it to a dictionary keyed by tag and returns True, or returns False if the tag is already there, keeping the first; count_by(inventory, field) returns a dictionary counting records by "item" or "room"; summary_lines(inventory, duplicates, invalid) returns the report as a list of lines: how many were accepted, duplicate and invalid, each problem with its line number, and the counts by item and by room in alphabetical order. Test each function with assert, including a duplicate in other capitals, a line with an empty part, a line with four parts and an empty inventory. Run it on a mixed set of entries and on none. On your phone, put the entries in a list in the program and run it in “Step through a program” (the lab can't answer input()); on a computer, read them with input() until a blank line. Then write about 150 words: why the inventory is a dictionary keyed by tag and not a list, and how many steps a duplicate check of 2,000 entries takes by comparing every pair, and with your dictionary.

en: Warm-up (3 min): Write LAB-003,microscope,B12 and lab-003, Microscope ,b12. Decide: one microscope or two, and why?
Normalise (6 min): Rewrite eight made-up entries with tag and room in capitals, item in small letters, spaces removed.
Check (6 min): Go down the list keeping a table of tags seen. Mark each duplicate and invalid line with its number.
Count (5 min): Count the accepted items by room, in alphabetical order. Then run this lesson's parse step and compare.
ar: التمهيد (٣ دقائق): اكتب LAB-003,microscope,B12 وlab-003, Microscope ,b12. قرّر: مجهر واحد أم اثنان، ولماذا؟
التوحيد (٦ دقائق): أعد كتابة ثمانية مدخلات متخيَّلة: الرمز والقاعة بحروف كبيرة، والصنف بحروف صغيرة، بلا مسافات.
الفحص (٦ دقائق): امشِ على القائمة مع جدول للرموز التي رأيتها، وعلّم كل مكرّر وكل سطر غير صالح برقمه.
العدّ (٥ دقائق): عُدّ الأصناف المقبولة بحسب القاعة مرتّبة أبجديًا، ثم شغّل خطوة parse في هذا الدرس وقارن.

note.en: Paper is enough for the first three steps: the phone checks your parse.

prompt.en: What does this program print?
prompt.ar: ماذا يطبع هذا البرنامج؟

explain.en: Indexes count from 0, so data[1] is the second value, 8, and data[-1] is the last, 15. len() counts the values: 3. Go back to lesson 1, Lists, indexing and iteration.
explain.ar: يبدأ عدّ الفهرس من 0، فـ ⁦data[1]⁩ هي القيمة الثانية، 8، و⁦data[-1]⁩ هي الأخيرة، 15. وتعدّ ⁦len()⁩ القيم: 3. ارجع إلى الدرس ١، القوائم والفهرسة والمرور عليها.

prompt.en: backup = items makes a separate copy, so backup.append("scale") leaves items as it was.
prompt.ar: تصنع ⁦backup = items⁩ نسخة منفصلة، فتترك ⁦backup.append("scale")⁩ القائمة items كما كانت.

explain.en: backup = items gives the same list a second name, so appending through backup changes items too. For a separate list, write backup = items.copy(). Go back to lesson 1, Lists, indexing and iteration.
explain.ar: تعطي ⁦backup = items⁩ القائمة نفسها اسمًا ثانيًا، فالإضافة عن طريق backup تغيّر items أيضًا. ولقائمة منفصلة اكتب ⁦backup = items.copy()⁩. ارجع إلى الدرس ١، القوائم والفهرسة والمرور عليها.

prompt.en: Match each campus job to the structure that suits it best.
prompt.ar: صِل كل مهمة في الجامعة بالبنية الأنسب لها.

left.en: The order students arrived at a lab
Each module's room, by module code
IDs already scanned at the exam door
left.ar: الأرقام التي مُسحت عند باب الامتحان

explain.en: Arrivals keep their order: a list. A room is found by a key, the module code: a dictionary. “Has this ID been scanned?” is the question a set answers in about one step. Go back to lesson 3, Choosing a structure, and counting the work.
explain.ar: ترتيب الوصول يُحفظ: قائمة. والقاعة تُوجد بمفتاح، رمز المقرر: قاموس. و«هل مُسح هذا الرقم؟» هو السؤال الذي تجيب عنه المجموعة في نحو خطوة. ارجع إلى الدرس ٣، اختيار البنية وعدّ الشغل.

prompt.en: counts = {"a": 2}, then counts["b"] = counts.get("b", 0) + 1, then counts["a"] = counts.get("a", 0) + 1. What are counts["a"] and counts["b"]?
prompt.ar: ⁦counts = {"a": 2}⁩، ثم ⁦counts["b"] = counts.get("b", 0) + 1⁩، ثم ⁦counts["a"] = counts.get("a", 0) + 1⁩. ما قيمة ⁦counts["a"]⁩ و⁦counts["b"]⁩؟

explain.en: get("b", 0) gives 0 for the missing key, so b becomes 1 with no KeyError. get("a", 0) gives a's 2, so a becomes 3. Go back to lesson 2, Dictionaries, lookup and counting.
explain.ar: تعطي ⁦get("b", 0)⁩ القيمة 0 للمفتاح الناقص، فتصبح b مساوية 1 دون خطأ KeyError. وتعطي ⁦get("a", 0)⁩ القيمة 2 لـ a، فتصبح 3. ارجع إلى الدرس ٢، القواميس والبحث بالمفتاح والعدّ.

prompt.en: This program counts room bookings, but it stops with a KeyError on the first room. Which line is wrong?
prompt.ar: يعدّ هذا البرنامج حجوزات القاعات، لكنه يتوقّف برسالة KeyError عند أول قاعة. أيّ سطر فيه الخطأ؟

explain.en: The first time a room appears it isn't a key yet, so counts[r] stops with a KeyError (on the phone: KeyError: B12). counts.get(r, 0) gives 0 then. Go back to lesson 2, Dictionaries, lookup and counting.
explain.ar: في أول مرة تظهر فيها قاعة لا تكون مفتاحًا بعد، فتتوقّف ⁦counts[r]⁩ برسالة KeyError (وعلى الهاتف: KeyError: B12). أما ⁦counts.get(r, 0)⁩ فتعطي 0 عندها. ارجع إلى الدرس ٢، القواميس والبحث بالمفتاح والعدّ.

prompt.en: items = ["laptop", "scale"]. What does items[len(items)] do?
prompt.ar: ⁦items = ["laptop", "scale"]⁩. ماذا تفعل ⁦items[len(items)]⁩؟

explain.en: len(items) is 2, but two values have indexes 0 and 1, so items[2] doesn't exist: IndexError: list index out of range. The last value is items[len(items) - 1]. Go back to lesson 1, Lists, indexing and iteration.
explain.ar: تساوي ⁦len(items)⁩ العدد 2، لكن للقيمتين الفهرسين 0 و1، فلا وجود لـ ⁦items[2]: IndexError: list index out of range⁩. وآخر قيمة هي ⁦items[len(items) - 1]⁩. ارجع إلى الدرس ١، القوائم والفهرسة والمرور عليها.

prompt.en: Finish the room count. It reads entries typed TAG,ITEM,ROOM, normalises each room, then prints each room and its count in sorted order, such as B12 2.
prompt.ar: أكمل عدّ القاعات. يقرأ مدخلات بالشكل TAG,ITEM,ROOM، ويوحّد كل قاعة، ثم يطبع كل قاعة وعددها مرتّبة، مثل B12 2.

hint.en: Normalise the room with strip() and upper(), or b12 counts apart from B12.
hint.ar: وحّد القاعة بـ ⁦strip()⁩ و⁦upper()⁩، وإلا عُدّت b12 منفصلة عن B12.

hint.en: Print in sorted order: for room in sorted(counts):. The phone won't keep the order rooms arrived.
hint.ar: اطبع مرتّبًا: ⁦for room in sorted(counts)⁩:. فالهاتف لا يحفظ ترتيب وصول القاعات.

hints.en: After the loop: for room in sorted(counts): print(room, counts[room]).
hints.ar: بعد الحلقة: ⁦for room in sorted(counts): print(room, counts[room])⁩.

explain.en: Normalising first makes b12 and B12 one room; get counts each room from 0; sorted() gives a report in room order. This joins lesson 4 (normalise) and lesson 2 (count with get, report sorted).
explain.ar: التوحيد أولًا يجعل b12 وB12 قاعة واحدة، وتعدّ get كل قاعة من 0، وتعطي ⁦sorted()⁩ تقريرًا مرتّبًا بالقاعات. يجمع هذا السؤال الدرس ٤ (التوحيد) والدرس ٢ (العدّ بـ get والعرض المرتّب).

prompt.en: The faculty's inventory has 2,000 entries to check for duplicate tags. Which statements are true? Choose all that apply.
prompt.ar: في جرد الكلية 2,000 إدخال يجب فحصها بحثًا عن رموز مكرّرة. أيّ العبارات صحيحة؟ اختر كل ما ينطبق.

text.en: A dictionary keyed by tag needs about 2,000 lookups
text.ar: يحتاج قاموس مفاتيحه الرموز إلى نحو 2,000 بحث مباشر

text.en: With 4,000 entries, every pair takes about twice as many comparisons
text.ar: مع 4,000 إدخال تأخذ مقارنة كل زوجين نحو ضعف المقارنات

text.en: Checking tag in a list of seen tags is one step per tag
text.ar: فحص tag في قائمة الرموز التي رأيتها خطوة واحدة لكل رمز

text.en: Every pair of 10 entries is 45 comparisons
text.ar: كل زوجين من 10 مدخلات يساوي 45 مقارنة

explain.en: Every pair of n is n × (n − 1) / 2: 1,999,000 for 2,000 and 45 for 10. A dictionary or a set needs one lookup per entry: 2,000. Doubling the entries makes every pair about four times bigger, and in on a list checks the list one by one. Go back to lesson 3, Choosing a structure, and counting the work.
explain.ar: كل زوجين من n يساوي ⁦n × (n − 1) / 2⁩: أي 1,999,000 لـ 2,000، و45 لـ 10. ويحتاج القاموس أو المجموعة إلى بحث مباشر واحد لكل إدخال: 2,000. ومضاعفة المدخلات تجعل مقارنات كل زوجين أكبر بنحو أربع مرات، وتفحص in على القائمة عناصرها واحدًا واحدًا. ارجع إلى الدرس ٣، اختيار البنية وعدّ الشغل.

prompt.en: A student's inventory normalises tags with upper() but forgets strip(). Entries arrive as "LAB-001" and "lab-001 ". How many records does it keep?
prompt.ar: يوحّد جرد أحد الطلاب الرموز بـ ⁦upper()⁩ لكنه ينسى ⁦strip()⁩. وتصل المدخلات ⁦"LAB-001"⁩ و⁦"lab-001 "⁩. كم سجلًّا يحتفظ به؟

text.en: 2: the space makes a new tag
None: it stops with an error

explain.en: upper() gives "LAB-001" and "LAB-001 ", which still differ by the trailing space, so the duplicate slips in as a second record. Normalising needs both: strip(), then upper(). Go back to lesson 4, The equipment inventory.
explain.ar: تعطي ⁦upper()⁩ القيمتين ⁦"LAB-001"⁩ و⁦"LAB-001 "⁩، وما زالتا تختلفان بالمسافة في النهاية، فيدخل المكرّر سجلًّا ثانيًا. والتوحيد يحتاج إلى الاثنين: ⁦strip()⁩ ثم ⁦upper()⁩. ارجع إلى الدرس ٤، جرد الأجهزة.

prompt.en: Fill the gaps so the program prints how many different tags there are, ignoring capitals and spaces. It should print 2.
prompt.ar: املأ الفراغين ليطبع البرنامج عدد الرموز المختلفة، دون اعتبار للحروف الكبيرة والمسافات. يجب أن يطبع 2.

explain.en: The list comprehension normalises every tag: LAB-001, LAB-001, LAB-002. set() keeps each once, so len() gives 2; list() would keep the repeat and give 3. This joins lesson 4 (list comprehension, normalise) and lesson 3 (sets).
explain.ar: توحّد list comprehension كل رمز: LAB-001 وLAB-001 وLAB-002. وتحفظ ⁦set()⁩ كل قيمة مرة واحدة، فتعطي ⁦len()⁩ العدد 2، أما ⁦list()⁩ فتحفظ المكرّر وتعطي 3. يجمع هذا السؤال الدرس ٤ (list comprehension والتوحيد) والدرس ٣ (المجموعات).

title.en: Activity: Explain it to a friend

en: Answer (10 min): The ten questions, on paper first.
Mark (3 min): Check each answer with the app.
Go back (5 min): For each miss, reread its lesson.
Explain (4 min): Tell a friend one idea you fixed.
ar: الإجابة (١٠ دقائق): الأسئلة العشرة، على الورق أولًا.
التصحيح (٣ دقائق): تحقّق من كل إجابة في التطبيق.
العودة (٥ دقائق): لكل خطأ، أعد قراءة درسه.
الشرح (٤ دقائق): اشرح لصديق فكرة صحّحتها.

en: Answer (10 min): Answer all ten questions on paper before you open the app. Write a prediction for every line of code.
Mark (3 min): Answer them in the app and compare. Circle each question you got wrong.
Go back (5 min): Each explanation names a lesson. Reread that lesson's reading, or replay its video chapter.
Explain (4 min): Explain one idea you got wrong, and why, to a friend, or write it in two sentences.
ar: الإجابة (١٠ دقائق): أجب عن الأسئلة العشرة على الورق قبل أن تفتح التطبيق، واكتب توقّعًا لكل سطر كود.
التصحيح (٣ دقائق): أجب عنها في التطبيق وقارن، وضع دائرة حول كل سؤال أخطأت فيه.
العودة (٥ دقائق): كل شرح يذكر درسًا. أعد قراءة نص ذلك الدرس، أو أعد مشاهدة فصل الفيديو.
الشرح (٤ دقائق): اشرح لصديق فكرة أخطأت فيها ولماذا، أو اكتبها في جملتين.

note.en: Predict on paper first: a wrong prediction you can explain is worth more than a lucky answer.
note.ar: توقّع على الورق أولًا: فالتوقّع الخاطئ الذي تستطيع شرحه أنفع من إجابة صحيحة بالحظ.
